name: Gravel
seoDesc: Gravel: work out length from the width and the area. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: length is what the Gravel calculator works out, and it gets there from the width, the area, the price per unit of mass and the total cost. It is built for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Gravel calculator work?
sections.html:
The Gravel calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports length in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the gravel type); then you type in the width, the area, the price per unit of mass and the total cost.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 17 options, such as regular gravel, gravel (dry) and gravel (dry, 1/4 - 2”). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Gravel calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Length=area ÷ width
Depth=volume needed ÷ area
Volume needed=weight needed ÷ density
Weight needed=total cost ÷ price per unit of mass
Volume needed=total cost ÷ price per unit of volume
Price per unit of volume=density × price per unit of mass

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Gravel type set to Gravel (dry, 1/4 - 2”). Straight away the calculator returns Density = 1680000 kg/m³.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Density = 1680000 kg/m³ should be roughly the size you expected from Gravel type set to Gravel (dry, 1/4 - 2”).

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in cubic meters, and convertible to any of the 40 units on that chip.
  • Shown in metric tons, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilograms per cubic meter, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Mass, opening in metric tons
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Gravel calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the width, the area and the price per unit of mass — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Gravel calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns length, derived from the width, the area and the price per unit of mass. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Gravel calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the width, the area, the price per unit of mass and the total cost, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter density in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Density opens in kilograms per cubic meter and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Density = 1680000 kg/m³. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Gravel calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
